title: Holi: the festival of colors
hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali before dawn in the South, Krishna breaking open Naraka's fortress. Your line was light the way home. Did you help someone out of a tight spot? Day six hundred eighty-one.

A little boy runs to his mother, upset. Why is Radha so fair, he asks, and I'm so dark? It isn't fair. His mother, smiling, has an idea. Go and color her face, she says, any color you like. Then you'll match. The boy is Krishna, the mother Yashoda, and that small story, told and sung all over the Braj country where Krishna grew up, is one of the reasons people there say Holi began. Last time, Holi was Prahlad's fire. Today, it's Krishna's color.
screen: `WHY IS SHE FAIR AND I'M DARK?` → `GO AND COLOR HER FACE.` → `KRISHNA'S COLOR.`

segments.voice: Braj is the region around Mathura and Vrindavan, south of Delhi, where Krishna's childhood stories are set. And in Braj, Holi isn't one day. It's a season, stretching over a week or more. In Barsana, the village tradition remembers as Radha's, there's Lathmar Holi, Holi of the sticks. Men from Nandgaon, Krishna's village, come over to throw color, and the women of Barsana meet them with long sticks and beat them, playfully, while the men hide under shields and everyone sings. The next day, it happens the other way around in Nandgaon. In Vrindavan's temples, there's a day when priests throw flower petals instead of powder over the crowd. And everywhere, songs about Krishna and Radha and the cowherd girls, the gopis, drenching each other with colored water. Poets in Braj Bhasha, the local language, wrote hundreds of Holi songs over the centuries. The Prahlad story and the Krishna story don't compete. Many families tell both: the fire the night before, for Prahlad, and the colors the next day, which in Braj belong to Krishna. And notice what the Krishna story is about underneath the play. A boy notices a difference between himself and someone he loves, and it bothers him. The answer isn't to argue about it. It's to throw color until nobody can tell who's fair and who's dark, who's from Barsana and who's from Nandgaon. Under all the color, the faces are level.
screen: `BRAJ: KRISHNA'S COUNTRY.` · `LATHMAR HOLI: STICKS AND SHIELDS.` · `PETALS IN VRINDAVAN'S TEMPLES.` · `PRAHLAD'S FIRE, KRISHNA'S COLOR.` · then, large: `UNDER THE COLOR, THE FACES ARE LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle the breath. Think of someone you feel slightly apart from: different age, different politics, different background, someone you're a little guarded around. Picture both of your faces covered in the same bright pink powder, so nobody could say which is which. Notice if anything loosens. If there's a small grudge with them, let it slide off with the color. The bell holds the time.
Holi. In Braj it's Krishna's season of color, with sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan, and every face the same bright mess.
Your line: everyone's the same color today. Today, find one thing in common with someone you usually feel different from. Day six hundred eighty-one.

fork.setup: you're Yashoda. little Krishna is upset that Radha is fair and he is dark. what do you tell him?
options: that it doesn't matter, so stop asking.
to go and color her face.
that he'll grow out of it.
fork.reveal: in the story, she tells him to color Radha's face any color he likes, and people in Braj say that's how Holi's colors began.

original.note: Hindi lāṭhī (stick) + mār (beat) + holī: Barsana's Holi of the sticks.

trapdoor: what you thought: Holi has one story behind it.
what it means: it carries Prahlad's fire and, in Braj, Krishna's colors, told side by side.
what a scholar hears: the Radha and Yashoda story is a popular and devotional telling, sung in Braj Bhasha Holi songs, rather than a scene from the Bhagavata Purana.
